national.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
national.summary: The verdict follows a months-long trial in New York.
national.body:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

In a statement, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

national.summary: Reporting from the Louisiana State Penitentiary, 60 Minutes contributor Sebastian Junger interviewed inmates who are still in prison after being convicted by a non-unanimous jury, a practice the U.S. Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in 2020.
national.body: Last week, while visiting a rodeo in the Louisiana State Penitentiary, also known as Angola, 60 Minutes contributor Sebastian Junger met some men who are behind bars even though the jury's verdict wasn't unanimous in their cases. One of them, Kenny Palmer – nicknamed "300" – sells art and crafts at the rodeo, which has been dubbed the "Wildest Show in the South." He makes chess boards, wooden jewelry and other crafts by hand. Palmer hopes to send some of the profits to his niece.Almost 20 years ago, Palmer was sentenced to life without parole for killing a man in a drug deal. The jury at his trial was split 10-2, with two voting not guilty. But Palmer was still convicted under a Louisiana law, which, at the time, allowed for non-unanimous jury convictions, or split jury convictions. "The only Black woman on there [and] the one elderly White woman voted not guilty," Palmer told Junger in an interview. Palmer said prosecutors have an unfair advantage when split jury convictions are allowed. "You're able to convict me with a reasonable doubt…. I'm supposed to be given either a new trial or be given a plea bargain," he told Junger. "The non-unanimous jury system is like fighting a 10,000-pound silverback gorilla on steroids. Real talk. How can you win?" Palmer said. Non-unanimous juries date back to 1880 and were created to dilute Black voices in the justice system.The practice was enshrined in the Louisiana Constitution in 1898 during a constitutional convention that hoped to "establish the supremacy of the white race in the state."Then, in 2020, the United States Supreme Court declared non-unanimous jury convictions unconstitutional.Oregon and Louisiana were the only states that allowed split jury convictions at the time. The Supreme Court ultimately left it up to the states to decide whether the ruling would apply retroactively. national.title: Trump's Nvidia intervention ties his political fortunes to the AI boom
national.summary: The US president's intercession to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang has inextricably linked their fates.
national.body:
After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised first clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

The alert said some people within 5 miles southwest of the plant may be evacuated and told people up to 20 miles away to stay indoors with windows closed. Officials expect the wind to blow southwest, away from Burlington, a city of just under 25,000 people on the Mississippi River.The Army moved the detonation from Friday, citing more favorable wind and time to add safety measures, according to a government court filing. A federal appeals court cleared the way Monday for the detonation after it had been delayed several times amid lawsuits from environmental groups and concerns from elected officials in Illinois and Iowa.The maps show the modeled lead dust from 9 a.m. until 5 p.m. Wednesday. At 9 a.m., a red circle is centered near the plant. By 9:45 a.m., the shaded area becomes a long oval running from near Burlington southwest toward the Missouri line.By early afternoon, the shaded area stretches far into northeast Missouri, passing Knox City. By late afternoon, it narrows to a band running from the Burlington and Keokuk area toward Macon, Missouri, with Quincy, Illinois, just southeast of it. Wind arrows on the maps point southwest. Illinois officials said Monday that NOAA's latest model showed no Illinois counties would be affected. The Illinois EPA had asked the Army for updated modeling but had not received it, officials said, and Gov. JB Pritzker has directed state agencies to remain on alert.Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said state agencies are setting up additional monitoring of air and water quality.The maps are forecasts and will change with the weather. Under the EPA's permit, the Army must update its plume forecasts six hours before the detonation and hourly after that until it is finished. national.title: Man on cruise ship goes overboard off Bahamas, search underway
national.summary: The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday.
national.body: Officials are searching for a man who went overboard during a cruise vacation on board Royal Caribbean's Allure of the Seas, according to Bahamian officials.The Allure of the Seas is on an eight-day Thanksgiving cruise in the Caribbean that departed from Miami on Sunday. The cruise line called out a passenger's name over the ship's loudspeaker system for several hours before determining that the man had gone overboard, according to passengers on board the cruise ship. The ship then turned around to look for him, the passengers said. The ship's captain announced Monday that the crew had "received a report of a missing guest" earlier in the day before determining "that the guest had unfortunately gone overboard," according to two recordings of a captain's announcement obtained by CBS News.Christian Bunse, a passenger aboard the ship, told CBS Miami, "People got quiet when they heard it, because they heard his name again."Royal Caribbean told CBS News that it "immediately launched a search and rescue effort" to find the man and are working with authorities.The Coast Guard said the Allure of the Seas alerted it and the Royal Bahamian Defense Force of a man overboard at around 11:30 p.m. on Monday. The Coast Guard said the man was reported to have gone overboard off the coast of San Salvador Island, Bahamas. The Royal Bahamian Defense Force is leading search efforts for the man, aided by the Coast Guard. "We are coordinating with the cruise and will have a vessel on scene," said a spokesperson for the Royal Bahamas Defence Force. Royal Caribbean said its care team is providing "support and assistance to the guest's loved ones." A woman fell from her balcony on the Allure of the Seas on a Taylor Swift-themed cruise in October 2024. Dulcie White's family alleged in a lawsuit that Royal Caribbean's unlimited drink package encouraged overconsumption, and that crew members ignored clear warning signs before the fatal fall. Her body was never recovered. The case remains ongoing.

national.summary: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 68 drums of lead azide in Iowa despite local leaders and residents raising concerns.
national.body: The U.S. Army's plan to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa has been delayed multiple times amid a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume for miles.The Army said the controlled detonation of lead azide is necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own."Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement. President Trump said Monday that without the demolition, "a very dangerous situation exists," but ordered the Army to defer its plans until a ruling came down from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials. The Army said it modeled four different ways to try to neutralize the chemicals, and concluded that a controlled detonation was the best method available. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commander of the operation, said Tuesday. "It would be irresponsible for us to not take the determined, consensus-based course of action moving forward."The government has argued the detonation — which is expected to send a plume of toxic lead particles into the surrounding area — is necessary because the lead azide could spontaneously explode."There is consensus across the experts, across the country, that a controlled mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to an uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance," Telle said Tuesday.A federal appeals court on Monday declined to block the Army from detonating the explosives. national.body: A day after President Trump intervened to reinstate Nvidia's embattled CEO, a new report suggests that Trump himself may have benefited financially to the tune of millions of dollars. White House correspondent Liz Landers reports. Amna Nawaz: Tonight, the fallout from Nvidia's leadership shakeup is putting President Trump's personal financial interests in the spotlight. A day after Mr. Trump intervened to reinstate the AI giant's embattled CEO, a new report suggests the president himself may have benefited financially to the tune of millions of dollars. Geoff Bennett: We will take a closer look at what's next for Nvidia in a moment. But, first, for more on the president's involvement, we're joined by our White House correspondent, Liz Landers. So, Liz, what is known about President Trump's financial stake in Nvidia, and his history of trading at stock while in office? Liz Landers: This president is the first to actively trade individual stocks while he's in the presidency. This is breaking a norm, and it's led to a lot of questions, not just about Nvidia, but about other companies that he owns stake in as well. The issue with these stock disclosures is the range here. So, based on a November 5 filing, the president owned between 32,000 and 370,000 shares of Nvidia. That's a huge range there, which means he gained between $1.3 million and $15 million from yesterday's surge when Jensen Huang returned as a CEO. CNBC says that, in his second term, Trump has bought or sold Nvidia stock at least 103 times. And they point out that some of the specific timing of these trades is notable. One example of this, in May, President Trump sold between a half-million and a million dollars of Nvidia stock right after he came back from this visit to China that he did. And, apparently, before that visit to China, he was briefed that Jensen Huang had this relationship with this suspected Chinese spy. Analysis shows that the president buys and trades Nvidia stock fairly regularly. national.body: A federal magistrate judge questioned whether prosecutors had probable cause for at least two of the offenses they were investigating when they sought to search the Washington, D.C., home of Democratic Minnesota U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, according to court documents released Monday evening. The records, which cover last month's raid, reveal a behind-the-scenes constitutional dispute between federal prosecutors and U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh. The judge's questions about probable cause surface in a filing prosecutors made Oct. 7. The specific statutes are redacted. The Justice Department expressly disclaimed any connection to Omar's congressional office, describing the investigation as concerning private conduct, not legislative activity. But the judge, who raised the question independently after reviewing the warrant application, concluded that Speech or Debate Clause protections for members of Congress apply to a search of Omar's home. Prosecutors had argued the privilege covers only congressional offices and certain electronic devices. "That logic does not hold," Sharbaugh wrote. Sharbaugh also rejected prosecutors' reasoning about how likely it was that congressional materials would be kept at Omar's home, writing: "That perspective blinks reality." The judge noted that many professionals bring work home and that a lawmaker's work happens in many places. The judge also required the Justice Department to modify its search procedures. Prosecutors had offered two alternative protocols, but the judge found both fell short because agents would have searched before Omar, even with a lawyer present, had a chance to identify legislative materials. The judge required that Omar have an opportunity to identify constitutionally protected legislative materials before investigators searched for them. The judge also rejected the government's suggestion that such protections would make lawmakers immune from prosecution. The majority of the 169 pages of court documents are heavily redacted and consist of exchanges between federal prosecutors and a magistrate judge over probable cause, constitutional privilege, warrant execution and public unsealing. national.title: States sue HUD over a rule that would end housing aid for mixed-status families
national.summary: HUD defends the rule, saying it prevents illegal immigrants from exploiting eligibility requirements.
national.body:
Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press Mikella Schuettler, Associated Press

Twenty-one states and Pennsylvania's governor have sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development over a rule that would deny federal housing assistance to families if any household member lacks eligible citizenship or immigration status.

The states say the rule could split up families or evict U.S. citizens from public housing. States including California, New York, Arizona and Massachusetts joined the suit. HUD defends the rule, arguing illegal immigrants are taking advantage of the current eligibility requirements.

The rule takes effect on Dec. 14. It would require people to verify their citizenship or eligible immigration status to receive federal housing assistance.

"No child should lose their home over a parent's immigration status," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference. "This rule is cruel, and it's unlawful."

For over three decades, Congress has authorized prorated federal housing assistance for mixed-status families, whose members have different citizenship or immigration statuses. These families receive less assistance if a household member is ineligible because of their immigration status. The new rule would ban mixed-status families from receiving any assistance.

"Picture a mom with two kids in public housing. All U.S. citizens. Their dad is not eligible. Under this rule, all four of them lose their home," Bonta said.

One in five children in California is part of a mixed-status family, said Bonta, estimating that the rule will affect 7,000 households in his state. The new rule would also require public housing authorities and private landlords to report tenants who fail verification to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

national.title: Florida politician says son's killing was not a 'freak hunting accident'
national.summary: Carey Washington Vinson, 19, was inside his tent at a camping site near the Blackwater River in Florida when a bullet struck him in the head.
national.body:
A Florida politician whose teenage son was fatally shot during a camping trip with friends says the shooting was an act of "malicious intent", not a "freak hunting accident".

Joe Vinson, a newly elected county commissioner in Florida, said his son Carey Washington Vinson, 19, was inside his tent near the Blackwater River in Florida when a bullet struck him in the head.

"As we understand it, some person(s) stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun at the sandbar campground, knowing it was occupied," Vinson said in a post on Instagram.

The local sheriff's office has asked the public for help in identifying any suspicious activity at the campground.

Police said they responded to an emergency call about a shooting and found the victim at a campground in Holt, Florida, with a gunshot wound to the head. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

Santa Rosa County Chief Deputy Randy Tifft told US media that a vehicle was parked on the other side of the river at the time of the shooting and that witnesses saw it leave after the gunfire.

Vinson, who was recently elected as commissioner in Escambia County, issued a statement saying he needed to "correct a misimpression" that the shooting was an accident.

"This was not a freak hunting accident — not someone firing carelessly in the dark," the teenager's father said in his social media post.

national.title: Paxton drops Texas lawsuits that accused doctors of illegally providing transgender youth care
national.summary: May Lau and M. Brett Cooper were among three doctors who Paxton called "scofflaws" and "radical gender activists" in lawsuits that threatened to impose steep fines and revoke their medical licenses.
national.body:
Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press

DALLAS (AP) — Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is ending efforts to punish two doctors who were among the first in the U.S. to face accusations of violating bans on providing care to transgender youth, dropping the cases as the Republican prepares to leave office following a failed Senate run.

The lawsuits against the doctors, which were filed in 2024, were among a spate of high-profile cases that helped Paxton burnish his image as a conservative fighter but are now winding down as Democrats prepare to retake power in Texas for the first time in decades.

The state's lawsuits against May Lau and M. Brett Cooper were dismissed Friday, according to attorneys for the doctors. They were among three doctors who Paxton called "scofflaws" and "radical gender activists" in lawsuits that threatened to impose steep fines and revoke their medical licenses.

"Dr. Lau did nothing wrong, but she was a convenient scapegoat for the Attorney General's Office, which issued press release after press release about its case — a case that has now collapsed," Nicole LeBoeuf, an attorney for Lau, said in a statement.

LeBoeuf said the timing of the dismissal after Paxton's loss "validates that this case against Dr. Lau was political from beginning to end." Lau moved her medical practice from Dallas to Oregon during the lawsuit.

Paxton's office did not immediately return a request for comment Monday.

Paxton, a close ally of President Donald Trump, dropped another lawsuit last year against a third doctor, Hector Granados, and his office later said the El Paso pediatric endocrinologist did not break the law.

national.title: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
national.summary: Nvidia's share price have fallen 7% as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's reinstatement.
national.body:
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.

In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .

But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

national.title: U.S. jury finds Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud
national.summary: Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries under U.S. sanctions and making false statements to officials.
national.body:
Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press Michael R. Sisak, Associated Press

Larry Neumeister, Associated Press Larry Neumeister, Associated Press

NEW YORK (AP) — A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.

However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy. The charge typically is used in organized crime and drug cases, but prosecutors used it to accuse Huawei of operating in an illicit fashion to steal intellectual property from American companies.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The verdict followed a lengthy trial in which U.S. prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the U.S. and elsewhere.

Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.

Lawyers for the company said U.S. investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei's more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn't actually exist.

national.title: How tariffs, fuel and fertilizer costs are squeezing the U.S.'s biggest apple region
national.summary: Washington's $9 billion industry grows more than 70% of the nation's fresh apples. Farmers are being pressed by high costs, tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.
national.body:
As Sean Gilbert stepped out of his white GMC pickup, he breathed in the scent of applewood and Columbia Basin dust. Here, just south of Wapato, Wash., one of his 50-acre Gala and Red Delicious apple orchards is ground into huge piles of mulch chips. The wood chipper is the size of a semi-truck and belts out a screeching racket.

He said this ground will lay fallow. It will cost this fifth-generation apple farmer less to leave it unplanted and weedy than to plant another orchard or crop. He scooped up a handful of applewood mulch. "It's a bit of a relief that we're not going to continue to be hemorrhaging dollars on orchards that the market doesn't want," he said. "It hasn't been making sense for a while."

Washington's $9 billion industry grows nearly 70% of the nation's fresh apples, according to Jon DeVaney, president of the Washington State Tree Fruit Association.

DeVaney said farmers are being pressed by the costs of labor, fuel, fertilizer, equipment, as well as weak exports from international tariffs and a strong dollar that diminishes foreign purchasing power.

He estimated thousands of acres of apple orchards across the Northwest are being rapidly torn out, or are not being actively cared for, because many farmers aren't making money growing the fruit. And after several years of similar economic conditions, many farms have gone deep into debt – with even some large, well-established operations filing for bankruptcy .

Andrea Starr Andrea Starr In this orchard, apples are often picked in the early hours of summer mornings to keep the fruit and workers cool. Andrea Starr hide caption

In the late summer and fall, unpicked apples have been left to rot in branches and on the ground. Over the past few years, an estimated thousands of acres have only been partially picked or not picked at all, according to Kate Tynan, senior vice president of the Northwest Horticultural Council , a trade association that advocates for the Northwest tree fruit industry on federal policy issues and international trade.

No one is happy with it Economy Farmers fear more damage from U.S.-Canada trade fight Politics Trump administration announces $12 billion in one-time payments to farmers Recent federal regulatory changes would effectively lower wages for some immigrant workers and take housing costs out of their paychecks. Tynan said with updates to the way wages are calculated, farm owners are hoping they'll be able to break even – but the farm workers union has pushed back on these changes and an upcoming federal judicial decision could put operators on the hook for backpay for the 2026 season.

national.title: The U.S. government is investigating Iranian ties to as many as 50 hacked commercial vessels
national.summary: The attacks, if officials who spoke to NPR are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the war with the U.S.
national.body:
The U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.

That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal .

The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.

Europe Iran denies it was behind cyber fridge attacks targeting France NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.

The Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.

The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts."

However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.

National Security A new cold war: hackers target fridges across the globe According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.

national.title: Pentagon sharply criticizes Canada over modernizing military
national.summary: The Defense Department accused Ottawa of failing to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.
national.body:
TORONTO (AP) — The Pentagon has accused Canada of falling short as a credible partner in defending North America, delivering a sharp rebuke over military spending and its reconsideration of American-made F-35 fighter jets.

In an unusually blunt fact sheet, the U.S. Defense Department on Monday said Ottawa had failed to make the tough decisions needed to modernize its military and meet NATO commitments.

"Canada's defense shortfalls speak for themselves," it said. "Canada must get serious and focused."

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada's defense minister, said Canada had committed 81.8 billion Canadian dollars ($56.9 billion) over five years to rebuild its armed forces and reached NATO's 2% defense spending benchmark five years ahead of schedule.

"Canada is also on track to meet NATO's new commitment to invest 5% of GDP annually in defense by 2035 and is taking concrete steps to build the capabilities needed to meet that goal," he said in a statement.

The Pentagon said U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was "laser focused" on modernizing Canada's military after decades of American taxpayers footing the bill for its defense.

Canada reached NATO's previous target of spending 2% of gross domestic product on defense and joined allies pledging to reach 5% by 2035, including related security investments. Its latest budget projects combined defense and security spending of 4.1% of GDP by 2027-28, but only 2.6% of GDP would go toward core defense.

The Pentagon accused Ottawa of having no credible, fully costed plan to meet NATO's 5% target and postponing the largest spending increases until after the 2029 federal election. Canada's parliamentary budget watchdog has also questioned how the government will meet the target.

national.title: Australia set to pass online safety laws with multibillion-dollar fines for tech giants
national.summary: The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms.
national.body:
MELBOURNE, Australia (AP) — The Australian government clinched a political deal on Tuesday to introduce online safety laws that could expose tech giants to multibillion-dollar fines for failing to prevent foreseeable online harms. The United States warned that the legislation would lead to censorship of lawful speech.

The Digital Duty of Care Bill would require Big Tech to proactively reduce the risk of harm before it occurs, according to an Australian government statement.

The legislation is similar to the European Union's Digital Services Act, passed in 2022, and the United Kingdom's Online Safety Act passed a year later.

The proposed legislation would set minimum safety standards for online services, including games, apps and artificial intelligence chatbots, requiring them to protect Australians from seriously harmful material and conduct, the government said.

"We can't cure the internet, but this is providing some basic safety standards and saying if you build it, you are responsible for its risks," Communications Minister Anika Wells told reporters at Parliament House in Canberra.

Wells announced on Tuesday her center-left Labor Party government had accepted amendments proposed by the minor Greens party to get the legislation through the Senate, where no party holds a majority.

Greens leader David Shoebridge confirmed his party had agreed to support the amended bill.

"Today we are taking power back from a handful of billionaire-owned, largely U.S. corporations and giving it back to Australians who have been paying too high a price for their profits," Shoebridge said in a statement.

national.title: Democrats supporting abortion rights won big in midterms, but vast changes unlikely soon
national.summary: States with bans will still have enough Republicans in power to likely block any repeal attempts for now.
national.body:
Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press Geoff Mulvihill, Associated Press

Democrats who ran on abortion rights platforms won big in elections for Congress and state government offices. But it's not likely that they'll be able to impose quick and vast abortion policy changes.

That's because Democrats did not take full control of the legislatures and governor's offices in states with the strictest laws — those that ban abortion at six weeks or all stages of pregnancy.

And in Congress, Democrats who will control both the House and Senate could attempt to bar states from adopting some kinds of abortion bans, but any move would likely meet a veto from President Donald Trump, which couldn't be overridden without GOP help.

Abortion has been primarily a state government issue since the U.S. Supreme Court's 2022 ruling that struck down Roe v. Wade allowed states to enforce bans. Now, 13 states ban abortion at all stages of pregnancy — with some exceptions — and four more do so after about the first six weeks.

In 2027, Democrats will have control of both legislative chambers and the governor's office in six states where they currently share power with Republicans. Those states — Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin — already allow abortion through until at least fetal viability, which is generally considered to be sometime after 21 weeks of pregnancy.

Abortion is currently allowed through the first 20 weeks from fertilization, or about 22 weeks' gestation in Wisconsin and 23 in Pennsylvania. Democrats kept the governorships and gained full power in the legislatures in the elections in both states.

Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro are both calling for leveraging that power to amend their states' constitutions to create a right to abortion.

national.title: DR Congo says military aircraft missing as rebels claim to shoot down plane
national.summary: A South African fighter pilot and a Ugandan officer are reportedly among those aboard the downed plane.
national.body:
The Democratic Republic of Congo military says it is searching for one of its aircraft, after rebels said they had shot down a warplane in the east.

The military said it had lost contact with a small Cessna 208 cargo plane on Sunday following "poor weather conditions". The fate of the plane and its crew remained uncertain, it added.

On the same day, the rebel Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) said it had shot down a plane of the same type that was on a mission to bomb Minembwe in South Kivu province.

Four people were reportedly on board, including a Ugandan and a South African pilot, who is said to have been captured alive.

On Tuesday, the FRN said the plane they had shot down was a Cessna 208, which had been "converted into a light attack aircraft" enabling it "to carry and launch precision-guided bombs and missiles".

Its wreckage now lies 10km (6 miles) from Minembwe, a rebel statement said, adding that a Ugandan and South African "mercenaries" had been captured.

The BBC has not independently verified the rebel claim, or whether the aircraft reported missing by the DR Congo military is the same one the rebels say they shot down.

South Africa's government has not commented, while Uganda's military has denied any involvement.

national.title: Nigerian monarch, 92, suspended after sexual assault claims
national.summary: The Emir of Daura is one of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, with politicians often trying to gain his support.
national.body:
One of Nigeria's best-known monarchs, the Emir of Daura, has been suspended from all official engagements and travel following allegations of sexual assault by a Polish tourist.

The visitor said Umar Farouk Umar, 92, had grabbed her chest during a tourism encounter and that she felt disgusted by the experience.

The allegation sparked widespread discussion across social media platforms, with many calling for the suspension of the emir and an investigation - calls the Katsina state government has now heeded.

Umar has not commented on the allegations or his suspension.

He is one of several emirs - a traditional role dating back to pre-colonial times - who still wield great cultural and religious influence in northern Nigeria, although they have lost their political power.

Daura, where Umar serves as emir, holds an extremely important position for the Hausa people who dominate northern Nigeria. It is widely regarded as their spiritual homeland and the origin of the Hausa royal lineage, serving as the core of Hausa origin mythology and the legitimate foundation of traditional authority.

Politicians routinely visit his palace for royal prayers and to gain his support.

On her Instagram page, the tourist said she had spent 30 days travelling around Nigeria before visiting the Emir's palace on 14 November.

local.summary: The five-year ban applies to toys like talking stuffed animals, dolls or robots and comes amid safety concerns about some of the conversations children are having with those objects.
local.body:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a bill Tuesday that places a moratorium on AI chatbots in children’s toys.

The five-year ban applies to toys like talking stuffed animals, dolls or robots and comes amid safety concerns about some of the conversations children are having with those objects.

California recently took similar action , and Pennsylvania is considering its own moratorium .

New York’s prohibition takes effect in 90 days, so Hochul warned parents about the potential risk of purchasing toys with chatbots for holiday gifts in the meantime.

She also indicated more AI safety proposals are coming as part of her State of the State address early next year.

“We'll set clear safety standards and put independent experts inside these companies to make sure that they're following the rules, and that we'll insist that humans remain in control, and with plans to contain the danger if something does go wrong,” Hochul said.

Toy manufacturing, sellers or operators of AI companions face $15,000 per day per violation of the ban, which would be enforced by the Attorney General.

The ban follows other legislation aimed at AI safety, including age verification and warnings labels on social media sites for users under 18. Those laws have faced legal challenges by groups representing big tech firms.

local.title: Monroe County proposal aims to prevent people from becoming homeless
local.summary: Project Home would provide some public assistance recipients with larger housing allowances to prevent them from becoming homeless.
local.body:
Monroe County wants to nearly double the amount of public assistance money it provides individuals and families facing homelessness. But it needs state approval to do so.

The county wants to shift $2.8 million in public assistance funds to the effort, which officials are calling Project Home. The program provides larger housing allowances — up to 60% of fair market rent — to public assistance recipients most at risk of becoming homeless It would assist up to 600 households.

"That additional support will be the difference between a family falling behind on rent, (or) staying current," County Executive Adam Bello said. "It could mean the parents keeping their children in the same home, in a stable home, in the same school, surrounded by the same friends and support systems."

The county also would use the money to help people who have been staying in shelters for a long time be able to transition to a permanent residence.

Project Home is Monroe County's way of addressing what has been a long-term, state-level problem with deficient public assistance. The state sets the schedule for public assistance grants, but it hasn't boosted the amounts in decades even though housing costs have greatly increased.

Currently, a family of four receiving public assistance gets $374 to cover rent. The federally-calculated market rate for an efficiency apartment in Monroe County is roughly $1,000.

"The result has been a system that pays to keep people in shelters instead of supporting stable permanent housing," Bello said. "We cannot expect families to find housing stability when the support designed to help them doesn't help."

During a news conference Tuesday, several Democratic legislators and community leaders spoke in favor of the proposal. Among then was Aqua Porter, executive of the Rochester-Monroe County Anti-Poverty Initiative.

local.summary: MINA — Two people, found outside with with burns suffered from a house explosion on the French Creek-Mina Road near Findley Lake on Sunday, remain hospitalized at UPMC Pittsburgh. local.body:
MINA — Two people, found outside with with burns suffered from a house explosion on the French Creek-Mina Road near Findley Lake on Sunday, remain hospitalized at UPMC Pittsburgh.

Just after 6 p.m, firefighters responded to a call and found the house at 2170 French Creek-Mina Road fully engulfed in flames. Companies from Findley Lake, Sherman, Clymer, Panama, North Lake, Greenfield Township and Ripley responded and were on the scene until after midnight.

Stanley Hose Company Fire Chief Matt Oehleck was one of the first on the scene. “The house was fully involved when I got there and the roof had already collapsed,” he said. “There were two people in the front yard and they had severe burns.”

Findley Lake was the first to arrive with an engine, he added.

Findley Lake Fire Department Second Assistant Chief Jeff Park also noted two people with life-threatening injuries were found outside the house. They were taken to UPMC Hamot in Jamestown and then transported to Pittsburgh. Park said it is not known if the victims made it outside on their own or if they had been blown out by the explosion. “The debris field was hundreds of feet wide,” he said.

The explosion has been attributed to a propane leak, most likely in the basement of the house, Park said. It is not known how the leak occurred or how the propane built up sufficiently to cause such an explosion. “It’s possible the residents were away and had just come into the house,” he said. “All it would take is the flip of a light switch.”

Oehlbeck said Chautauqua County EMS and Findley Lake EMS were on the scene, as well as the Chautauqua County Fire Investigation Team and the Sheriff’s Office.

Both Oehlbeck and Park said the firefighters were on the scene until about 12:30 in the morning Monday. “It took more than four hours to put the fire out,” Oehlbeck said. “The house was a total loss.”

local.summary: The Office of the State Comptroller has made yet another highly critical review of Dunkirk’s finances. The latest withering letter to City Hall from Albany’s fiscal watchdogs concerns the 2027 budget proposed by Mayor Kate Wdowiasz and currently under review by the Common Council. “Based on the resu
local.body:
The Office of the State Comptroller has made yet another highly critical review of Dunkirk's finances.

The latest withering letter to City Hall from Albany's fiscal watchdogs concerns the 2027 budget proposed by Mayor Kate Wdowiasz and currently under review by the Common Council.

"Based on the results of our review, we determined that certain significant revenue and expenditure projections in the proposed budget were unreasonable," the letter states.

"In addition, we determined that of the 10 recommendations in our November 2025 budget review letter, the city fully implemented only three recommendations," OSC adds.

The items implemented were council review of certain appropriations identified in OSC's 2025 review; working to submit a report detailing the amount and cause of deficits; and close monitoring of revenues and expenditures, with timely and properly authorized budget adjustments as needed, throughout the year.

However, according to OSC, council did not make updating and correcting city accounting records a priority; did not properly establish a budget calendar; and did not ensure the 2026 budget was structurally balanced with realistic estimates before adopting it.

The letter repeatedly criticizes Dunkirk's finances on many levels. It notes, "Our (2027 budget) review was significantly limited by the city's incomplete, inaccurate and unreliable financial information, and by the responsiveness and willingness of certain council members and city officials to meet with our auditors. For example, we contacted all five council members, but only the councilman-at-large (Nick Weiser) and two other council members met with us."

OSC's letter continues, "Due to the poor financial information, we could not complete certain review procedures or adequately assess the reasonableness of significant 2026 revenue and expenditure projections and certain estimates in the proposed 2027 budget. In particular, we could not effectively analyze revenue and expenditure trends, and verify the assumptions supporting budget estimates, due to the city's unreliable accounting and financial information."

entertainment.title: Dolly Parton’s sister reveals heartbreaking reason why music legend withdrew from family and friends in final months of life
entertainment.summary: The country music icon died after a brief battle with cancer in August.
entertainment.body:
Dolly Parton’s sister Stella Parton revealed the Grammy winner withdrew from her family as she became “more frail” amid her cancer battle .

“I walked through the journey with her, but as she got more and more frail, she didn’t want me to see her that way,” the country singer told Entertainment Weekly in an interview published Tuesday.

“She would have been very sad if she was dying and saw me upset, crying. She was sparing all of us the pain of watching that.”

Stella, 77, recalled her and Dolly’s tradition of chatting on the phone every Tuesday for “as long as [the latter] wanted to talk.”

The “I Will Always Love You” singer even called Stella to chat when she underwent an experimental treatment in Frankfurt, Germany, last year.

Stella told the outlet that she has kept the final voicemail Dolly sent her ahead of her death on Aug. 25 at the age of 80.

Stella also recalled the deaths of her siblings, i ncluding her brother Coy “Denver” Parton in July, saying, “It’s not that I feel that they left me or that I lost them. I know exactly where they are.”

“They’re with Mama and Daddy, so I’m at peace with that,” she added, referring to her parents, Robert Lee Parton and Avie Lee Parton.

After opening in first place last weekend with $119 million domestically and a global haul of $225 million, Lionsgate’s sixth film in the Hunger Games franchise is expected to continue its reign atop the box office. Playing in 4,018 North American theaters, Sunrise on the Reaping is expected to earn north of $60 million and could hit upwards of $80 million and beyond. The $150 million-budgeted film hopes to build on solid word of mouth, earning an A- CinemaScore and holding a 94 score from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes, along with a 68 from critics. Five Films Later, He's the Keeper of Panem Movies 'Hexed' Review: Hailee Steinfeld and Rashida Jones Lead a Disney Fantasy More Enchanting in Its Spectacle Than Its Storytelling

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is already off to a killer start this week, notching the highest-grossing opening Monday domestically in the history of the franchise that kicked off with 2012’s Jennifer Lawrence-led The Hunger Games . Sunrise on the Reaping collected $12.8 million on Monday, topping the $12.3 million for 2013’s Catching Fire . Over the weekend, Sunrise debuted with the fifth-biggest launch in Lionsgate history, which also ranked No. 5 among 2026 domestic openings for all studios. Its $56 million domestic sum on Friday gave the new prequel film the third-best debut Friday in franchise history, behind Catching Fire and The Hunger Games.

“I will sit patiently and wait for that phone call,” Lionsgate film chief Adam Fogelson told The Hollywood Reporter in a recent conversation about his hopes to work with author Suzanne Collins on bringing the franchise back to the big screen. Joseph Zada stars in the new movie as Haymitch Abernathy, whom Woody Harrelson portrayed for the first four titles.

Disney releases animated offering Hexed in 3,725 North American theaters on Wednesday, with the studio projecting a five-day opening around $45 million. Directors Fawn Veerasunthorn and Jason Hand’s movie, which carries a hefty budget north of $200 million, is expected to draw females and families, with the coming weeks clear of new animated competition until Paramount’s Angry Birds 3 in a month.

entertainment.title: Vanity Fair’s Taylor Swift hit piece spurs bellyaching across Condé Nast
entertainment.summary: A source claims Wintour didn't read the piece before it was published, and wants nothing to do with it.
entertainment.body:
Anna Wintour wants no part of Vanity Fair’s takedown attempt of Taylor Swift , a source familiar with the situation tells Page Six.

The rumor machine at VF parent company Condé Nast has turned “Red” hot in the wake of the piece — which cites interviews with 100 sources from Swift’s life, including high school classmates who accuse her of bullying behavior. Staffers in the corridors of One World Trade are scratching their heads as to why a flagship title would pick a fight with one of earth’s biggest pop stars.

A source claims Wintour “doesn’t want to be involved in any of this” and that Vogue’s head of editorial content, Chloé Malle , is grumbling that there was no reason to do a hit piece when there was “nothing there” in the first place.

However, a rep for Vogue and Wintour says “there is no truth to any of it.” Wintour knew full well about the spicy article before it published, as she does with all things that go in print under her reign.

Entertainment sources outside the building who want magazines to always play nice have their knives out, too, throwing around wild claims that VF editorial director Mark Guiducci’s head is on the chopping block. But a Vanity Fair spokesperson said “any notion that Mark’s job is in trouble is categorically false.” In fact, said a highly placed source inside One World Trade, “He’s a golden boy” at Condé Nast.

Malle is said to be concerned about “unnecessarily” burning a bridge with Swift , particularly when it comes to having her attend the Met Gala or securing a Vogue cover with the “Bad Blood” star. “It’s creating a lot of confusion that Condé is going after her in such an aggressive way for no reason,” a source said.

The piece is also not Wintour’s style. “She prefers access,” the person added.

For the fourth year in a row, Formula 1 took over Las Vegas , transforming the Strip into a three-day collision of sport, nightlife, celebrity culture, and over-the-top entertainment.

The 2026 Formula 1 Heineken Las Vegas Grand Prix arrived at the end of a banner season for the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team. Kimi Antonelli had already made history as Formula 1’s youngest-ever World Champion at 20 years old, while Mercedes secured its first Constructors’ Championship since 2021.

But two days before Antonelli and teammate George Russell raced through the streets of Las Vegas, they were competing in very different vehicles.

Organized by Marriott Bonvoy with Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, the Fountains of Bellagio were transformed into a Formula 1-inspired racecourse, where the drivers and five Marriott Bonvoy members raced custom speedboats across the hotel’s famed waters. The event was part of Marriott Bonvoy Moments , which offers members access to exclusive experiences through the travel program’s longtime partners, including Mercedes (Marriott Bonvoy members can also currently bid on packages to see Celine Dion in Paris).

Russell looked comfortable behind the wheel, smoothly maneuvering around the course, while Antonelli took a more chaotic approach, colliding with buoys, stalling his boat, and taking a few unexpected detours. The professional drivers ultimately lost to two Bonvoy members, who posted the fastest average time.

Afterward, Antonelli and Russell headed to the Mercedes Fan Hub on Bellagio Drive, where they tested their pit-stop skills and greeted fans. Across the Strip, Williams driver Carlos Sainz returned to ARIA Resort & Casino with his Smooth Operator Dance Lounge, while Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc met fans at Bellagio’s Ferrari boutique.

Formula 1’s growing popularity has increasingly turned Grand Prix weekends into multi-day cultural events, and Las Vegas pushes that formula to its extreme.

entertainment.title: Dolly Parton Estate Reveals Creative Team That Will ‘Preserve and Carry Forward’ Her Legacy
entertainment.summary: The team will be led by Steve Summers, who worked with the music icon for more than 30 years.
entertainment.body:
The Dolly Parton estate has announced the leadership of its creative team led by Steve Summers , who worked with Parton for more than 30 years and will serve as the estate’s creative director.

Summers will steer a team that also includes creative manager Riley Reed Hanratty , design specialist Vance Nichols and creative specialist Bradley Schnabel . Together, they will be responsible for the creative direction of the estate, “helping preserve and carry forward the unmistakable style, creativity and vision that defined Dolly’s legacy,” according to a press release.

Summers launched his professional career in 1991 as a singer and dancer at Dollywood, where he developed an interest in costume and set design before taking on additional creative responsibilities. In 2004, Parton brought on Summers to stage and choreograph her Hello, I’m Dolly Tour, and in 2006, he was named creative director of Dolly Parton Enterprises. In that role, he oversaw Parton’s personal wardrobe styling and visual creative direction encompassing costumes, album artwork, stage design, product development and other elements. Working closely with Parton, he and his team created hundreds of custom looks every year and preserved her existing wardrobe.

As creative director of Parton’s estate, Summers will bring his decades of experience working with the late star to a portfolio that includes the upcoming Broadway show DOLLY: A True Original Musical and other creative initiatives celebrating the icon. He will additionally work on projects with Dolly’s niece Danielle Parton, who was recently announced as an official brand ambassador for the estate.

Hanratty joined Parton’s team in 2018 and has held a number of roles. She started in alterations before joining the team tasked with digitizing Parton’s clothing, a process that included cataloging, photographing, describing and preserving garments. In 2022, she was named costume shop manager and head seamstress, working closely with Summers while overseeing Parton’s personal closet.

Nichols, a 30-year veteran of scenic and interior design, began freelancing for Parton in 2019 under Summers’ direction. He initially focused on wardrobe embellishments while also assisting with tours and other large events. Nichols joined the team full-time in 2018, with his role expanding to include set design and décor for photo shoots, TV appearances and commercials. He has also worked with Parton’s sister, Rachel Parton George, on redesigning and decorating some of her personal properties.

entertainment.title: Battlestar Galactica's Showrunner Loved One Scene The Sci-Fi Channel Wanted To Cut
entertainment.summary: Battlestar Galactica creator Ronald D. Moore explained on Katee Sackhoff's podcast that Syfy didn't like this slow, heartfelt scene, but he doubled down.
entertainment.body:
Syfy/YouTube Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover " Battlestar Galactica" is a sci-fi series that defines the genre , mixing heady, philosophical narratives with nuanced character-building. Few scenes exemplify that balance better than one in the Season 2 episode "Valley of Darkness." Starbuck (Katee Sackhoff) and Helo (Tahmoh Penikett) are on Caprica, and they stop by Starbuck's old apartment. Starbuck puts on a tape of her father playing piano — actually a Philip Glass song — and laments the fact that while everyone else is fighting to return home, she's fighting because it's all she knows.

It's a very slow scene, and it features several seconds without dialogue. Perhaps unsurprisingly, cable channel SyFy was not a fan. While appearing on Sackhoff's podcast , "Battlestar" creator Ronald D. Moore revealed that the network hated that scene "because it was slow, and they're not doing anything — shouldn't there be more action?" Their disapproval caused Moore to double down, inspiring him to make the scene even longer than intended.

Sackhoff described the scene as a great example of the "intentional" pacing of the series, which was much slower than previous projects she had worked on. Moore explained that he often had to fight to maintain this languid pace.

Syfy/YouTube Though the original "Battlestar Galactica," created by Glen Larson , was where it all began, Ronald D. Moore's take on the series has become the defining version of the story. Moore's series grounds the tale of intergalactic war in its characters, making them feel like real people rather than larger-than-life heroes — so much so that TVLine ranked the show the best Syfy series of all time .

Speaking with Katee Sackhoff on her podcast, Moore highlighted the importance of creating space for the characters' unvarnished humanity to shine through. He referenced a scene in the 1st episode of "Battlestar Galactica," called "33," in which Laura Roslin (Mary McDonnell) and Commander Adama (Edward James Olmos) are speaking on the phone. Adama is silent for a few beats, and Roslin asks if he's still there.

Moore explained that he fought for that scene because it's the kind of natural moment that happens all the time when you're not reading from a script. "I was always looking for those little pieces that made them more people, that made them more human beings that we could relate to," he shared. Unfortunately, this was exactly the kind of thing that executives pushed back against, as they tended to look for scenes that prioritized action.

entertainment.title: Chart Rewind: In 1956, ‘Blues’ Singer Marty Robbins Swept 3 Country Charts
entertainment.summary: The Grand Ole Opry stalwart reached a new plateau with a crossover special.
entertainment.body:
Arizona native Marty Robbins moved to Nashville in January 1953 on the same day that he joined the Grand Ole Opry, and it became a good fit as Robbins attained a new level of success, beginning with his single “Singing the Blues.” It rose to No. 1 on Billboard ’s Most Played C&W in Juke Boxes chart dated Nov. 24, 1956, making him the leader on all three of the magazine’s country lists. He occupied all three simultaneously for a total of 10 consecutive weeks.

“Singing the Blues” had spent a week at the summit on each of the other two country charts, Best Sellers in Stores and Most Played by Jockeys; it would top the Juke Box and Best Sellers hit parades 13 total weeks, while reigning 11 weeks on Jockeys.

Following his 1952 debut single “I’ll Go On Alone,” which became his first leader, Robbins would accumulate 16 total country No. 1s, concluding with 1976 release “Among My Souvenirs.” The seventh of those singles, “Don’t Worry,” spent 10 weeks in the pole position, his only other single to reach double digits at No. 1.

Robbins picked up “Blues” from songwriter Melvin Endsley, who had contracted polio at age three and would be confined to a wheelchair for the remainder of his life. Robbins recorded the song in November 1955, and Columbia released it the following August. “Blues” also went to No. 17 on Billboard ’s pop Juke Boxes chart, where Guy Mitchell’s version reached No. 1, among reigns on other pop lists.

Robbins ultimately joined the Country Music Hall of Fame in October 1982, two weeks before he died from a heart attack.

entertainment.title: The Rings Of Power's Ancalagon The Black Explained: Who Killed Tolkien's Mightiest Dragon?
entertainment.summary: The latest episodes of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power have referenced the mighty dragon, Ancalagon the Black. Here's how Ancalagon died.
entertainment.body:
Ben Rothstein/Prime Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Contains spoilers for "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 — "The Lady of Lórien"

As Middle-earth struggles in "The Rings of Power" Season 3, Episode 5 , we finally learn a bit more about what happened to Galadriel's long-lost husband Celeborn. He's spent thousands of years in prison after being caught by the forces of evil in the final days of epic warfare that defined the First Age of J.R.R. Tolkien's world. At one point in the story, Galadriel says, "They told me you were dragon-fire." Celeborn responds that while dragon fire was a concern, he was knocked into some water by a horse right before "Ancalagon set my legion ablaze."

The name is a reference to Ancalagon the Black. The Index of Names at the end of "The Silmarillion" defines the character thusly: "Greatest of the winged dragons of Morgoth." Then we get the line: "Destroyed by Eärendil."

Translation: The greatest fire-breathing dragon to ever live in Middle-earth was killed by Elrond's father. The deadly encounter occurred in a world-changing, era-ending conflict called the War of Wrath, which was the final showdown between the angelic guardians of Arda (Tolkien's name for Earth), called the Valar, and the original Dark Lord Morgoth. There aren't a lot of details about the war. "The Silmarillion" says, "Of this march of the Host of the Valar to the north of Middle-earth little is said in any tale." One of the key features of that epic encounter, though, is the airborne duel between Eärendil and Ancalagon.

Prime Video In the War of Wrath, also called the Great Battle, the Valar attacked Morgoth in his mighty fortress Angband, which was built into the volcanic mountains called Thangorodrim in the northern regions of Middle-earth. When Morgoth's hosts are mostly defeated, the Dark Lord unleashes a last desperate assault, including, for the first time, winged dragons. (Earth-bound dragons feature a lot before this, but the flying serpents are a novelty.) At first, the fiery surprise attack works. "The Silmarillion" says the host of the Valar is driven back, "for the coming of the dragons was with great thunder, and lightning, and a tempest of fire."

This is where we meet Ancalagon, yet his time on Tolkien's stage is brief; he's only really mentioned once in "The Silmarillion." Right after the winged dragons are introduced, Eärendil shows up on his flying ship with one of Tolkien's legendary jewels known as the Silmarils strapped to and shining from his brow. Eärendil arrives with a host of flying creatures, including the Great Eagles (one of which already showed up in "The Rings of Power" this season) , at his back. The book says, "There was battle in the air all the day and through a dark night of doubt." Then we get the lone Ancalagon mention: "Before the rising of the sun Eärendil slew Ancalagon the Black, the mightiest of the dragon-host, and cast him from the sky; and he fell upon the towers of Thangorodrim, and they were broken in his ruin."

The reality star—who's appeared alongside BFF Khloe Kardashian and twin sister Malika Haqq on The Kardashians and Keeping Up With the Kardashians over the years—detailed her personal earnings in court documents pertaining to her ongoing divorce with ex Bobby McCray .

In an August filing obtained by E! News, Haqq—who broke up with McCray in 2023 after 13 years of marriage—listed her average monthly income in 2026 as $5,241, with another $437 a month in residuals.

And while she has almost $11,500 in savings, the 43-year-old said in court documents that her earnings are "not sufficient" in paying for household expenses for herself and McCray's three kids Christian , 15, Celine , 12, and Kapri , 5.

According to Haqq's filing, her household's average monthly expenses total to $13,892, which includes $4,512 on rent, $1,900 on groceries and $4,658 on school tuition for her and McCray's two daughters.

The Dash Dolls alum also said that she spends roughly $1,176 a month on debt payments, including outstanding medical costs for the birth of Kapri and a credit card bill with a balance of over $11,000. However, she has yet to make a payment on a $30,000 loan from her sister and an $80,000 loan from a "friend," according to her filing.

Haqq is requesting child and spousal support from her ex, whose monthly income she estimates is around $18,645.

In her filing, she said McCray—who retired from professional football in 2010—receives monthly payments of $11,250 in NFL disability and $2,829 as part of the league's annuity disbursement program. Moreover, she claimed McCray also receives $3,044 per month in social security disability. (McCray most notably suffered a bulging disc in his spine during the 2009 season with the New Orleans Saints.)

Haqq argued in court docs that McCray is "more than capable of meeting his own monthly expenses while simultaneously contributing toward" herself and their kids' expenses.

entertainment.body:
Apparently, 2Pac was over the back-and-forth with The Notorious B.I.G. , especially the East Coast/West Coast narrative.

E.D.I. Mean, member of the Outlawz and the slain rapper’s friend and collaborator, recently sat down with with Drink Champs and revealed that 2Pac was contemplating ending his vitriolic beef with his former friend.

He then said that Pac was planning on making an album that would’ve featured rappers from across the country in order to ease the tension between the two rivaling coasts. And so, prior to that, and before we started on Makaveli , we was working on One Nation ,” he continued. “I was privy to a lot of conversations him and his mother had. We all was. He had a plan to do songs with everybody from all over the country because he didn’t like the fact that this had turned into an East Coast/West Coast thing.”

E.D.I. Mean also said that it was ‘Pac’s mom Afeni Shakur that helped him start to see things from a different perspective and used her experience dealing with the U.S. government as a Black Panther as a reference point. “His mother was telling him about how COINTELPRO was able to wedge a separation in the Panthers by selling letters from the East Coast to the West Coast and vice versa, which led to the killings of people like Bunchy Carter and on the UCLA campus,” he said. “And so she was telling ‘Pac, ‘This is what they did to us.'”

entertainment.summary: "We stand firmly against this kind of inhumane treatment," the band wrote after masked agents detained a father and daughter
entertainment.body:
Pearl Jam called out ICE agents for their “inhumane treatment” of two people arrested at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport over the weekend.

Videos of masked ICE agents arresting Sofia Hernandez Meija and her father, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, have gone viral and sparked protests in Pearl Jam’s hometown of Seattle. Sharing an image of demonstrators, the band wrote, “It is heartbreaking and infuriating to watch the human toll of a system driven by cold cruelty. Seeing a family torn apart and dragged off a jetway right here in our own airport by masked individuals is unconscionable and we stand firmly against this kind of inhumane treatment.”

entertainment.title: Disney Sued for Allegedly Using Unlicensed Music in Social Media Ads: ‘Never Paid a Dollar’
entertainment.summary: The new case is one of dozens brought against brands over music on Instagram and TikTok, but none have targeted a media giant like Disney.
entertainment.body:
The latest in a flood of lawsuits over music on social media is targeting the Walt Disney Co. — and claiming that the Hollywood giant should have known better.

In a case filed Tuesday (Nov. 24) in Detroit federal court, Zac Hiller and his LAA Music claim Disney illegally used three of the publishing company’s songs across seven social media videos even though the entertainment colossus “never asked for a license” and “never paid a dollar.”

“For a hundred years, The Walt Disney Company has taught the world one rule: if you want to use what someone else created, you ask permission and you pay,” Hiller’s attorneys write. “Disney enforces that rule against everyone else. This case is about Disney exempting itself from it.”

The Disney posts were broadcast to “audiences in the millions,” the lawsuit says, including a promotion for Hulu that garnered 481,700 likes and 17,500 shares. The lawsuit claims the posts were removed after complaints, but that taking them down is not enough: “Taking a video down after getting caught does not undo the infringement.”

While many of the lawsuits have come from Universal Music, Sony Music or Warner Music, Tuesday’s case was filed by Hiller, an NFL agent and founder and CEO of the agency Loyalty Above All, which counts players like James Cook, J.K. Dobbins, and Shemar Stewart on its client roster.

The case claims that Disney used three songs owned by Hiller and LAA Music, including “Take it Off ‘Lights Off’ Beat”; “New Opp (beat)”; and “Gang Gang.” Three songs were allegedly used by ESPN, one by Hulu, one by FX and two more by Disney Parks.

“Disney negotiates synchronization licenses every day [and] employs people whose job is to clear music,” Hiller’s attorneys write. “Its infringement here was not the oversight of a company too large to notice. It was a business decision: use the music now, take the promotional benefit, and make the rights holder chase it later.”

Neither side immediately returned requests for comment on Tuesday.

entertainment.body:
Ninajirachi adores her computer more than almost anything — she said as much on her eclectic debut album, I Love My Computer . But the Australian electronic artist and producer wanted to turn the dial up further. How could she max out all the love she has in her heart? With the help of some friends.

“Most of my time making music is spent alone, so hearing these songs reimagined by an amazing lineup of artists has been really inspiring and emotional,” Ninajirachi said. “For an album that was written about experiences I’ve had all on my own, I Love My Computer has connected me to people all around the world more than anything else ever has. Ninajirachi wrote her message from Mexico City, where she’d connected with even more people who she first crossed paths with through music online. “There is no time I’d rather be alive than right now. I’m so grateful to the artists for bringing so much of themselves to every new version,” she said. “Some are new friends, some I’ve known since I released my first song as Ninajirachi. Meghan Markle’s father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been indicted on child pornography charges in California, just days after a Florida judge determined that he is mentally fit to stand trial .

Thomas Sr., 82, has been charged with two counts of possession of child pornography and faces up to 40 years in prison if convicted.

The indictment was shared on X by Bill Essayli , the United States Attorney for the Central District of California, who noted that Thomas Sr. stands accused of “knowingly” possessing “35mm film negatives of sexually explicit material involving children.”

“Federal law enforcement was notified last month that Markle possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in the Philippines and at two storage units in Los Angeles,” Essayli continued in his statement. “A judicially approved search warrant was executed and the materials were seized.”

The indictment refers to several specific frames that were uncovered by the FBI and that contain “at least one image of child pornography [that] involved a prepubescent minor and a minor who had not attained 12 years of age.”

Thomas Sr., who is currently being detained in Florida, “is expected to be arraigned on the indictment in the coming weeks in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles,” Essayli continued.

“This is an ongoing investigation. Markle is presumed innocent until proven guilty,” he concluded, while asking anyone with any knowledge of those involved with child pornography materials to contact the FBI.

entertainment.summary: “Torn” earns Parton her highest-ever Country Airplay debut and brings U2 to two Billboard country charts for the first time.
entertainment.body:
Dolly Parton ’s final recording is making its mark across multiple Billboard charts, as her collaboration with U2 , “Torn,” arrives on country and rock rankings (dated Nov. 28), while standing as one of the top-selling songs in the United States.

The song becomes the legend’s first posthumous entry on Hot Country Songs as it debuts at No. 39 with 1.6 million official streams, 1.2 million in radio airplay audience and 6,000 sold Nov. 13-19, according to Luminate. It marks U2’s first appearance on the ranking.

(Parton first made Billboard ’s charts in 1967; U2, in 1981.)

On the Nov. 21-dated Country Airplay chart, “Torn” opened at No. 28, securing Parton her highest-ever debut and introducing U2 to the survey.

Meanwhile, “Torn” enters Hot Rock & Alternative Songs at No. 24, becoming Parton’s second and top-charted hit on the tally, surpassing “World on Fire” (No. 26, 2023). The collaboration also launches at No. 2 on Billboard’s all-genre Digital Song Sales chart.

The track closes U2’s Carnaval De Luz , which debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with 49,000 equivalent album units, becoming the band’s 14th top 10. The set also opens at No. 1 on Top Rock Albums, Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales and No. 2 on Top Album Sales, Top Rock & Alternative Albums and Top Alternative Albums.

Produced by longtime U2 collaborator Jacknife Lee, the 12-track collection is the band’s first album of new material in nine years and its 16th studio LP.

The team-up took shape when Parton offered U2 an unfinished song of her own . U2 frontman Bono and Snow Patrol’s Johnny McDaid subsequently reworked Parton’s original tale of a woman torn between two men into the story of a mother and her two estranged sons, divided by political differences.

Jennifer Lawrence isn't letting speculation cloud her vision.

The Hunger Games star poked fun at theories that she'd recently undergone an eyelid surgery commonly referred to as an upper bleph, which have gained traction online since her return to the big screen for Sunrise on the Reaping .

Responding to her makeup artist Shayna Gold sharing a special delivery of Lawrence's new haircare line, Mes, the actress wrote on Instagram Stories Nov. 23, "iykyk she's the one who did my bleph."

The 36-year-old's one-liner referred to an upper blepharoplasty, a procedure that reconstructs the upper eyelid area, including the skin, socket and fat surrounding the eyelid. According to the National Institutes of Health , it's one of the most common operations done to the face.

Her comment appeared to shut down fan rumors—which were fueled by Gold's recent post of a photoshoot where she styled Lawrence's makeup—that she had elective plastic surgery to reduce her hooded lids. While the Red Sparrow actress didn't deny receiving the procedure outright, her cheeky response hinted that her new appearance is all thanks to makeup instead.

And when it comes to cosmetic alterations, the Oscar winner has previously divulged her latest beauty upgrades, including her decision to receive breast implants this year.

"They’re new," she told Andy Cohen on WWHL , adding of her cup size, "It’s a full C, I think. It’s the same size that they were."
